executive_summary: August 2026 paints a split picture: investors are broadly optimistic about where stocks will be a year from now and strikingly confident that any dip would bounce back fast — yet crash anxiety actually increased, and many still see the market as expensive. It's a bit like planning a beach vacation while eyeing the storm radar.

key_findings.headline: Optimism Rebounds for Institutions
key_findings.interpretation: Institutional confidence snapped back to 85.71% after dipping to 66.67% in July, while individual confidence eased slightly to 72.22% from 80.0%. This may reflect institutions responding to fresh data or simply reverting to a longer-term bullish stance after a one-month wobble.

key_findings.headline: Crash Worries Quietly Growing
key_findings.interpretation: Only 30% of institutional investors and 22% of individuals feel confident a crash won't happen — both readings down from July. In plain terms, a clear majority in each group now sees a meaningful chance of a sharp downturn in the next six months.

key_findings.headline: Near-Universal Dip-Buying Faith
key_findings.interpretation: Every single institutional respondent — 100% — believes a 3% daily drop would fully recover within two days, and individual investors nearly match at 87.5%. This is a dramatic surge from July's 45% readings for both groups, suggesting deep trust in the market's short-term resilience.

key_findings.headline: Valuation Views Still Divided
key_findings.interpretation: Two-thirds of institutional investors say stocks aren't overvalued, up from 60% in July, while only 40% of individuals agree — essentially unchanged. Some institutional respondents may hold an efficient-markets view, in which the current price is by definition correct, making 'overvaluation' a moot question.

detailed_analysis:
The standout number this month is buy-on-dips confidence. Jumping from roughly 45% in July to 100% among institutions and 87.5% among individuals is a remarkable shift. One reading of this: investors may believe that underlying market liquidity and momentum are strong enough to absorb any short-term shock almost instantly. Another possibility is that recent quick recoveries from minor sell-offs have trained respondents to expect the pattern to continue.

At the same time, crash confidence moved in the opposite direction — both groups are more worried about a major downturn than they were a month ago. That combination sounds contradictory but could make sense: investors may believe the market can shrug off small tremors while still fearing the kind of large, systemic event that doesn't obey normal recovery patterns. Think of it as trusting the brakes on your car but still worrying about black ice.

The gap between institutional and individual 1-year outlook widened again. In July, individuals were actually more optimistic than institutions — an unusual flip. August reverted to the more typical pattern, with 85.71% of institutions expecting gains versus 72.22% of individuals. Whether institutions were reacting to specific macro data or simply correcting what they saw as an overshoot in July's pessimism is hard to say from the numbers alone.

Valuation confidence tells an increasingly familiar story: institutions are more comfortable with current price levels than individuals are. The 40% reading among individuals has barely moved in three months, suggesting a persistent unease about whether stocks have gotten ahead of themselves. That said, the concept of 'overvaluation' is itself debatable — some institutional investors subscribe to the view that in a reasonably efficient market, the current price already reflects all available information, so labeling it overvalued is beside the point. Both perspectives have deep intellectual roots.
methodology: These indices come from the Yale/Shiller U.S. Stock Market Confidence Surveys, which have tracked investor sentiment since 1989. Each month, roughly 100 wealthy individual investors and 100 institutional investment managers answer the same standardized questions. The consistency of those questions over 35+ years is what makes the data meaningful — you can actually compare investor psychology across very different market environments. The four indices each measure something distinct: • 1-Year Confidence: The share who expect prices to be higher in 12 months. • Crash Confidence: The share who believe a crash in the next 6 months is very unlikely (under 10% probability). A low reading means most people think a crash is plausible. • Buy-on-Dips Confidence: The share who believe that after a 3% single-day market drop, prices would fully recover within two days. • Valuation Confidence: The share who do not believe the market is overvalued. Surveys were conducted semi-annually before 2001 and have been monthly since July 2001. Respondents rotate over time, but consistent characteristics — high income, investment experience — are maintained across the panel.
